report:
**Conclusion: generally no.** Arthroscopy—typically joint washout (lavage), trimming damaged tissue (debridement), or partial meniscus removal—does **not meaningfully improve pain or function from knee osteoarthritis** beyond good non-surgical treatment, and it exposes patients to surgical risks and recovery.

**Why the answer is no:**
- In a placebo-controlled trial (including sham surgery), arthroscopic debridement or lavage did not improve pain or function versus placebo. Cochrane’s review likewise concludes debridement probably does not improve pain or functional ability compared with placebo. [Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD005118_arthroscopic-debridement-osteoarthritis-knee)
- A later randomized trial in people with moderate-to-severe OA compared optimized physical/medical therapy with the same therapy plus lavage/debridement; surgery added no worthwhile benefit. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18784099/)
- The broader, updated Cochrane review of arthroscopy for degenerative knee disease (OA, often with degenerative meniscal tears) found the procedure remains common despite guidelines strongly recommending against it. [Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease)
- Accordingly, AAOS says lavage/debridement arthroscopy is **not recommended** when the primary diagnosis is knee OA (moderate-strength recommendation). [AAOS guideline PDF](https://www.aaos.org/globalassets/quality-and-practice-resources/osteoarthritis-of-the-knee/oak3cpg.pdf)

This does not mean arthroscopy is never appropriate: an orthopedist may consider it for a *separate*, specific problem—such as a truly locked knee from a loose body or an acute traumatic tear—not simply OA pain, stiffness, or an MRI finding of degenerative meniscal tearing.
